name: Nebbiolo

lines.s10: Nebbiolo makes Barolo and Barbaresco, a pale red that smells of tar and roses and grips like a far darker wine.
lines.s20: Nebbiolo is the red grape of Barolo and Barbaresco, from the Langhe hills of Piedmont. It looks pale, but its sour cherry, rose petal and tar ride on high acidity and a tannin that wants years, or a braised dish.
lines.s45: Nebbiolo looks gentle and is not. It is the grape of Barolo and Barbaresco, from the Langhe hills around Alba in Piedmont. The glass is pale garnet, with sour cherry, rose petal and tar, but the tannin grips hard and the acidity is high. The law holds Barolo back for more than three years, and many cellars still age it in large old casks that add little taste of wood. Pour it with braised beef, a mushroom risotto or anything under white truffle. Its name is thought to come from nebbia, the fog that fills the valleys when it is picked in October.
lines.sale: Nebbiolo smells as delicate as a rose and grips like a far darker wine, and with food that grip turns to pleasure. I would decant a Barbaresco now and pour it with the braised beef.

glass.lead: Sour cherry, rose petal and tar in a pale garnet glass, over high acidity and a firm, drying tannin.

ladder.where: Valtellina, Carema, and Gattinara and Ghemme in the north
Barolo, Barbaresco and Roero, around Alba

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin high and drying, alcohol medium plus to high, body medium plus to full, and pale in colour for all that.

home.home: Piedmont, above all the Langhe hills around Alba, where Barolo and Barbaresco are Nebbiolo alone, aged for years, often in large old casks. Roero across the Tanaro is softer. In the north it is Spanna in Gattinara and Ghemme, and Chiavennasca on the terraces of Valtellina in Lombardy.
home.abroad: Abroad it is rare. Australia grows it in the King Valley and the Adelaide Hills, and California and Baja California a little; these tend to be softer and fruitier, and some Baja vines so named are not Nebbiolo.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, a cool room temperature.
service.glass: A wide Burgundy bowl, which gathers the rose and tar perfume.
service.decant: Consider it for a young Barolo after tasting a sample; decant an old one gently off its sediment.
service.age: Barolo and Barbaresco ten to thirty years, and they need them; most Langhe Nebbiolo within five.

with.why: slow cooked fat and protein meet the firm tannin

with.dish: Egg pasta with shaved white truffle
with.why: the truffle meets the wine's own truffle and rose
savoury depth beside dried cherry and tar
salt and fat round off the grip

labels.means: Nebbiolo alone from the hills south west of Alba, aged at least 38 months, 18 of them in wood.
Nebbiolo from lower, warmer hills north east of Alba, aged at least 26 months, 9 in wood.
Nebbiolo from the wider Langhe, released young: a lighter, earlier way into the grape.
Nebbiolo's names in northern Piedmont and in Valtellina, Lombardy.

guest.q: It looks so light. Why does it feel so strong?
guest.a: Nebbiolo carries little of the pigment that makes a red look deep, so it is pale and turns orange at the rim early. The power is in its tannin and acidity, not its colour.

guest.q: What is the difference between Barolo and Barbaresco?
guest.a: The same grape from neighbouring hills. Barbaresco lies lower and a little warmer, north east of Alba, ages for a shorter time by law and is often open sooner. It is not a lesser Barolo.

guest.q: Is this young Barolo ready to drink tonight?
guest.a: It will still grip. A decanter lets the perfume open, and a rich, slow cooked dish makes the tannin feel gentler. Left ten years or more, it softens and truffle and leather come through.

compare.tell: Pinot Noir is as pale but silky, with softer tannin and red cherry; Nebbiolo adds tar, higher acidity and a drying grip Pinot lacks.
Sangiovese is a little deeper, with tomato leaf and dried oregano and less tannin; Nebbiolo is paler, with tar and roses and a bigger grip.
Xinomavro shares the pale colour, high acidity and firm tannin, but brings sun dried tomato and black olive where Nebbiolo has tar and a fuller scent of roses.

cards.front: Nebbiolo: where is it at home, and what are its other names?
cards.back: Piedmont: Barolo, Barbaresco and Roero around Alba, Gattinara and Ghemme in the north. It is Spanna in northern Piedmont and Chiavennasca in Valtellina, Lombardy.

cards.front: Nebbiolo blind: which pairing of colour and structure gives it away?
cards.back: Pale garnet, orange at the rim, over high tannin and high acidity, with tar and rose petal on the nose. It looks light and drinks powerful.

cards.front: Nebbiolo as Barolo and as Barbaresco: the minimum ageing of each?
cards.back: Barolo 38 months with 18 in wood, Riserva 62. Barbaresco 26 months with 9 in wood, Riserva 50. Counted from the November after the harvest.

questions.q: A red poured blind is pale garnet with an orange rim, yet it grips hard: high tannin, high acidity, sour cherry, rose petal and tar. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: A pale colour hiding high tannin and high acidity, with tar and roses, is Nebbiolo. Pinot Noir, the nearest wrong option, is as pale but silky, with softer tannin and no tar.

questions.q: A guest who loves Barolo asks for the same grape in a lighter, more perfumed wine from the Alpine terraces of Lombardy. Which wine do you bring?
questions.exp: Valtellina Superiore is at least 90 per cent Nebbiolo, called Chiavennasca there: lighter and more perfumed than Barolo, and ready sooner. Barbera d'Asti, the nearest miss, is another grape, low in tannin.

questions.q: A guest asks why the Barbaresco on the list reached the market a year before the Barolo of the same vintage, though both are Nebbiolo. What is the reason?
opts: Its legal minimum ageing is shorter
It is aged in steel alone
It comes from younger vines by law
questions.exp: Barbaresco must age 26 months with 9 in wood, Barolo 38 months with 18, so Barbaresco is released sooner. Both are Nebbiolo alone, so softening with Barbera is the nearest wrong reason.

sources.title: Consorzio di Tutela Barolo Barbaresco Alba Langhe e Dogliani: Nebbiolo
Wine Companion: grape varieties and wine styles, Italian reds

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. Nothing contradicts TASTE.world old.

The cellar facts (Barolo 38 months with 18 in wood, Riserva 62; Barbaresco 26 with 9, Riserva 50; large old casks and the barrique of the 1980s), the names Spanna and Chiavennasca, the Valtellina Superiore rule of at least 90 per cent and two years, and Baja Nebbiolo warm, soft and not always Nebbiolo all stand on the Codex's own Piedmont, Lombardy and Mexico records.

The name from nebbia, fog: the consortium's own page gives it as one of two explanations (the autumn fog at the late October harvest, or the bloom that fogs the berries), and trade references agree; the line says is thought to come from.

The ladder takes two rungs, cool and moderate: the Court's grid reads Barolo and Barbaresco as moderate, and the Codex's Lombardy and Piedmont records call Valtellina and Alto Piemonte lighter and higher in acid. Nebbiolo has no warm home a guest meets on a list.
Abroad: the King Valley and the Adelaide Hills stand on two Australian trade sources; the sites could not be opened in this session, only read through search results, so a checker should open them.

Nebbiolo's profile in GRAPES gives the alcohol as high and the grid reads medium plus to high; the structure line follows the grid. Its other field writes TAR AND ROSES in capitals as a tell, which is its own style and no error.

checked.verdict: Sound after four fixes. The Barolo and Barbaresco rules, the northern names and the fog all stand; Australian Nebbiolo was called riper from two regions the Codex calls cool, a guest answer leaned on the decanter against the tannin, and two tells parted Nebbiolo from its neighbours by rose, which both carry.
changed: worlds.home.abroad: Riper was said of the King Valley and the Adelaide Hills, which the Codex calls cooler with elevation and cool; the trade sources call Australian Nebbiolo softer and more fruit forward, and the Codex's Mexico record calls Baja's warm, dark and soft. Softer and fruitier holds all of them.

guest.2.a: A decanter and a slow cooked dish were said to help a great deal against the grip, which comes near promising air against tannin, and the service reference never does. The decanter now opens the perfume and the dish makes the tannin feel gentler, as the Codex's pairing data puts salt and fat.

compare.0.tell: The tell parted Nebbiolo from Pinot Noir by rose petal, and the Pinot Noir entry lists rose petal among its own notes. Higher acidity, which the reviewed profiles give Nebbiolo and not Pinot Noir, takes its place.
compare.2.tell: The tell gave rose petal to Nebbiolo alone, and the Codex's Naoussa record gives Xinomavro dried rose. Tar stays the clean parting note and the rose becomes a matter of degree.
open: Wine Companion is the brand of a living writer, though neither its title nor its address names him; it is kept, as the second, fifth and sixth chunks kept it, and the integrator may weigh it.
The Aglianico entry's tell to Nebbiolo gives Nebbiolo red cherry where this entry and GRAPES give sour cherry; another author's fragment, left for its owner.
